title: Coroutine-based Benchmark Sampler Playbook
body:
Overview:

This playbook documents a coroutine-driven client sampler for throughput benchmarking and a set of priming/steady-state heuristics designed to improve repeatability while exercising KV-cache interactions. The goal is pragmatic: reduce run-to-run variance for occupancy-sensitive workloads while covering realistic bursty patterns we see in customers. This is intentionally different from our other loadgen playbooks—it focuses on the client-side scheduling primitives (coroutines + soft-token buckets) and the ways those primitives interact with per-request cache state and runtime batching.

Why coroutines?
- Lightweight concurrency lets us simulate many logical clients with minimal host CPU overhead.
- Easier to express jittered timers, cooperative backpressure, and staggered priming sequences compared to thread/process models.
- Integrates cleanly with async IO used by many of our internal SDKs.

Key Concepts and Terms:
- Sampler: coroutine scheduler that dispatches request work items based on an arrival model and per-client pacing rules.
- Occupancy: fraction of GPU capacity occupied by in-flight requests in a sliding window. Not the same as QPS; occupancy ties to latency & token-length.
- Priming window: initial period where we intentionally bias inputs to warm KV caches and kernel hot paths.
- Soft-token bucket: per-coroutine token budget subject to jitter and occasional borrow/repay semantics to simulate client burst tolerance.
- KV-cold vs KV-warm traces: two categories of input sequences to exercise cache-hit vs cache-miss behavior.

Architecture (high-level):
1) Driver process runs N coroutine workers. Each coroutine holds a microstate: client-id, local-cache-hint (boolean), sequence-length-hint, and token-balance.
2) Arrival model feeds coroutines with target inter-arrival distributions: poisson, lognormal-bursts, and tide-waves (sinusoidal envelope).
3) Coroutines schedule requests against a central pacing controller that enforces a global concurrency ceiling and emits occupancy telemetry.
4) Requests include a priming header that toggles model prompt prefixes to drive KV cache touches deterministically for the first M requests.

Recommended Configuration Snippets (human-friendly, not an exact YAML parser):
- harness: coroutine
- workers: 1024  # many light-weight coroutines to emulate thousands of clients
- global_concurrency: 128  # target in-flight on server side (adjust per GPU type)
- arrival: poisson, lambda=12/s  # per-worker mean; overall QPS ~ workers * lambda
- burst_profile: { type: lognormal, sigma: 1.2, burst_probability: 0.08 }
- priming: { length: 60s, kv_mode: stratified(80% warm-seq,20% cold-seq), phased: true }
- soft_token_bucket: { initial_tokens: 8, refill_rate: 1/s, max_borrow: 4 }
- seed_strategy: randomized-run-seed + run-label  # see reproduction section

Priming Heuristics (why they matter):
- Phase-based priming: rather than a single monolithic warmup, use small phases that mix warm and cold sequences to reduce pathologically long priming tails on kernels that are only touched by rare sequence lengths.
- Deterministic priming sequences for a run: derive priming sequences from the run-seed so that repeated runs with the same seed recreate the warm/cold mix.
- Staggered priming starts: launch coroutine groups with 2–5s offsets to avoid giant synchronized spikes that bias the runtime scheduler.

Repeatability Checklist (quick):
- [ ] fix run-seed in harness config (log seed to experiment metadata)
- [ ] fix docker/container image hash and runtime kernel versions
- [ ] pin model variant and quantization profile used for the run (model@vX)
- [ ] capture per-coroutine seed snapshot for reconstruction (optional for heavy debugging)
- [ ] save full trace of first 2 minutes of RPC headers (for KV-hit reconstruction)

Diagnostics & Telemetry to Capture (server + client):
- client: coroutine allocations, event loop lag, token-bucket borrow events, request timestamps, sampled payloads
- server: per-GPU occupancy (sliding 5s), kernel selection logs, KV-cache hit rate by prompt-hash, batch composition (seq-lens in batch), scheduler backpressure signals
- correlation keys: run-seed, coroutine-id, trace-id

Known Failure Modes and Mitigations:
- Synchronized priming spikes: if you see 10–20% latency spikes at start, add staggered start windows and reduce per-group worker count.
- High CPU on driver: reduce per-worker Python overhead by moving critical sampling hot paths into compiled Rust/Go loops or use ucontext-based coroutine pools.
- KV-cache warmup never reaches steady hit-rate: inspect priming coverage—increase diversity in warm sequences or lengthen priming window for rare lengths.
- Unstable occupancy despite identical seed: host-level noise (thermal throttling, CPU frequency scaling) often the cause—use dedicated bench nodes and capture host telemetry.

Experiment Recipe (example run for A100-style GPU):
1) Image: bench-harness:v2.3.1@sha256:abcd1234
2) Model: open-llama-13b@v3-quantized (pin exact config)
3) Workers: 512, global_concurrency: 96, arrival poisson lambda=10/s, priming 90s stratified
4) Run-seed: 20251104-01
5) Collect: 10m steady window after priming; store server metrics at 1s granularity and client trace for first 3m
6) Repeat: 5 runs with same seed and 3 runs with different seeds (total 8) to estimate within-seed vs across-seed variance

Post-run Analysis Tips:
- Compute occupancy percentiles rather than mean-only; tail occupancy correlates strongly with tail latency.
- Decompose variance: between-seed variance vs within-seed variance. If within-seed dominates, you likely have non-deterministic host factors.
- Use batch-composition histograms to see if batching regime changed across runs (e.g., more short-seq requests led to smaller batches and lower throughput).

Repro Strategy When Runs Diverge:
1) Re-run the first 30s trace in an isolated environment with tracing agent attached (kernel trace + host perf).
2) If divergence persists, decrease worker count and increase per-worker lambda to isolate scheduling boundaries.
3) Capture a binary artifact: client-recorded request vector for first N requests and replay with a single-threaded replayer to validate server determinism.

Lightweight Validation Checks (small script assertions to include in harness):
- assert total_requests_sent == sum(server.accepted + server.errors)
- assert median_batch_size within +/- 10% of target profile
- assert KV-hit-rate in primed window >= expected_threshold

Open questions / TODOs:
- We need a standardized compact on-disk format for first-minute traces so replays are trivial. (Ben to prototype: github PR linked above)
- Investigate coroutine switching overhead at Python-level vs green-thread libs. If overhead >1us per switch, consider compiled runtime sampler.
- Define canonical run labels and metadata fields to ensure bench results are importable into the Console perf dashboard.

Appendix: Suggested Quick CLI for local dev runs (pseudo):
$ python -m bench_harness.driver --mode coroutine --workers 256 --concurrency 64 --arrival poisson:lambda=8 --priming 60s:kv=stratified --seed 20251104-01 --out ./runs/20251104-01

Concluding notes:
This playbook is deliberately prescriptive about the client-side scheduling primitives because we found a number of hard-to-reproduce throughput anomalies when using heavyweight process-based drivers. The coroutine sampler gives us fine-grain control over jitter, borrowing semantics, and staggered priming that together produce a smoother steady-state occupancy distribution more representative of production traffic. Feedback welcome; propose we run a cross-team validation next quarter to compare coroutine sampler vs existing loadgens across three canonical workloads.

End of document.
